questions.question: Which formula defines the Riemann sum?
What is $x_i^*$ for a Riemann sum?
options: The only endpoint of $I$
The value of $S(f,P_n)$
The number of subintervals
Any point in $J_i$

questions.question: For $f(x) = 2$ on an interval split into subintervals with total length $5$, what is the Riemann sum?
In a regular subdivision of $[0,1]$ into $4$ equal subintervals, what is the width of each subinterval?
On what choices can a Riemann sum depend?
options: Both the partition and the sample points $x_i^*$
The partition only, since sample points cancel out
The sample points only, since the widths always sum to $|I|$
Only the number $n$ of subintervals, not their positions

questions.question: What do Riemann sums approximate?
options: They approximate accumulation by finite sums
They approximate the slope of $f$ by difference quotients
They approximate the maximum of $f$ by sampling points
They approximate infinite series by adding the first $n$ terms

questions.question: For $f(x) = x$ on $[0,1]$, use two equal subintervals and right endpoints. What is the Riemann sum?
If the same partition is used but a different sample point is chosen in one subinterval, what may change?
options: The definition of a set
The Riemann sum
The fact that $I$ is an interval
The notation $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Why is boundedness of $f$ part of the setting for the Riemann sum?
options: The definition assumes $f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ bounded on a bounded interval.
Because every function in mathematics is unbounded.
Because sample points are not allowed for bounded functions.
Because bounded functions cannot have Riemann sums.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why different Riemann sums may approximate the same integral?
options: Different partitions or samples always give exactly the same finite sum.
Different sums converge to different limits; the integral is their average.
Different partitions or samples give different sums with the same limit.
Only left and right sums approach the integral; other tags may not.

questions.question: For $f(x) = 1$ on any bounded interval $I$, which expression is the Riemann sum for any partition?
For $f(x) = x$ on $[0,1]$ with one subinterval and sample point $x_1^* = 0$, what is $S(f,P_1)$?
What does $|J_i|$ represent in a Riemann sum?
options: The value of $f$ at the sample point $x_i^*$
The number of subintervals in the partition
The length of the subinterval $J_i$
The length of the whole interval $I$

questions.question: What does a Riemann sum of $f$ over $[a,b]$ approximate?
options: The definite integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$
The derivative of $f$ at a point of $[a,b]$
The arc length of the graph of $f$
An antiderivative $F$ of $f$ on the interval $[a,b]$

questions.question: Which choices can make two Riemann sums for the same function differ?
options: The choice of partition or of sample points $x_i^*$
The order in which the rectangles are added up
Only the choice between left and right endpoint tags
Only whether the subintervals are open or closed

questions.question: For $f(x)=3$ on an interval split into subintervals with total length $2$, what is the Riemann sum?
For $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ with one subinterval and sample point $x_1^*=1$, what is $S(f,P_1)$?
For a regular subdivision of $[0,6]$ into $3$ subintervals, what is the common width?
Why does refining a partition usually improve a Riemann-sum approximation?
options: Each refinement makes the sum exactly equal to the integral
Smaller subintervals improve the approximation
More subintervals always increase the value of the sum
Refining raises the upper sum and lowers the lower sum

questions.question: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, use two equal subintervals and right endpoints. What is the Riemann sum?
